id        epic:commercial-clients
kind      epic
status    draft
title     Commercial clients
summary   A commercial client is a record of its own, belonging to exactly one account, with create, read, update and delete.
revision  3

# Commercial clients

A commercial client is a record of its own. It belongs to exactly one account. A caller can create,
read, update and delete a commercial client.

## What this rests on

Every line below cites the located fact it was read from. `path:line` citations come from the
`aep reverse scan` bundle of 2026-09-03 over commit `70a8b69`; nothing here is derived from a
source outside this repository.

- **There is an account, and it is a record with an identity.** `src/accounts.py:5` holds accounts
  in `_ACCOUNTS: dict[str, dict]`, keyed by an id minted at `src/accounts.py:10-11` as a
  `uuid.uuid4()` string and stored back onto the record as `account_id`. So "belongs to exactly one
  account" has an existing thing to point at, and an existing key to point at it with.
- **The account already has the full create/read/update/delete quartet.** `create_account`
  (`src/accounts.py:8`), `read_account` (`src/accounts.py:15`), `update_account`
  (`src/accounts.py:20`), `delete_account` (`src/accounts.py:29`), plus `list_accounts`
  (`src/accounts.py:35`). `README.md:5-9` states the same quartet in prose. The commercial client
  asks for the same four verbs, so this epic's shape is the shape the repository already uses, not
  a new one.
- **The store is in-memory and process-local.** `src/accounts.py:5` is a module-level dict;
  `README.md:3` says "An in-memory store for accounts and nothing else". There is no database, no
  serialisation and no transport layer in this repository, so a commercial client lands in the same
  substrate.
- **This repository has decided nothing about what happens to what an account owns.**
  `src/accounts.py:31` carries the only TODO in the tree — "deleting an account must decide what
  happens to whatever belongs to it" — and `README.md:11` raises it a second time under the heading
  "Not yet decided". `aep reverse history` dates that line to 2026-09-03, commit `70a8b69`
  ("Accounts service, never planned"): it is an open question the repository was published with,
  not rot.

## The consequence of that last citation

This epic introduces the first thing that *belongs to* an account. It therefore makes
`src/accounts.py:31` answerable for the first time — and it does not answer it. Whether deleting an
account cascades to its commercial clients, is refused while any exist, or orphans them, is a
product decision this repository does not record and I cannot read out of it. It is tracked as a
blocker rather than guessed.

## Out of scope, and why

- **Answering `src/accounts.py:31` for entities other than the commercial client.** Nothing else
  belongs to an account in this tree.
- **Listing commercial clients.** `list_accounts` (`src/accounts.py:35`) exists for accounts, but
  the stated outcome names create, read, update and delete only. Not drafted, and named here so the
  omission is visible rather than silent.
- **Persistence, transport, authentication.** No evidence in the tree (`aep reverse scan`: 0 API
  surfaces, 0 CI jobs, 0 task targets).

## Acceptance

A caller can create a commercial client against an existing account, read it back, update it and
delete it; a commercial client always carries exactly one account id; and the account-deletion
question at `src/accounts.py:31` has either been answered by a recorded decision or is visibly
blocked, never silently chosen.

## Domain

The noun this epic introduces now has a typed home, drafted 2026-09-03 and validated:

- `specification/system.yaml` — `ess/1`, system `accounts`, version `v1`.
- `specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` — `accounts.commercial_client.CommercialClient`,
  identified by `commercial_client_id`, carrying `account_id`, with a `references` relation of
  cardinality `one` to `accounts.account.Account` via `account_id`.
- `specification/domains/account.yaml` — `accounts.account.Account`, the relation's target, typed
  from `src/accounts.py:5-11`.

```console
$ ess validate --path specification
accounts v1 — 3 file(s), valid
```

Three things are marked `UNMAPPED:` in those files rather than guessed, and each blocks work:

1. **Whether an account owns its commercial clients, and with what cardinality.**
   `src/accounts.py:31` and `README.md:11` leave it open. `owns` against `references` decides
   whether a commercial client can survive its account; one-to-one against one-to-many projects a
   different schema. The commercial client's own side of the link is declared, because "belongs to
   exactly one account" is readable in the direction this epic states it; the inverse is not.
2. **Every attribute of a commercial client other than `account_id`.** The epic says a commercial
   client is "a record of its own" and never says what is on the record. While `account_id` is the
   only field, "update a commercial client" can only mean reparenting it, which is a different
   feature from editing it.
3. **Whether a commercial client has states.** Neither entity models one; `delete_account`
   (`src/accounts.py:29-32`) removes a record rather than moving it to a state.

## Decomposition

Decomposed 2026-09-03 into two stories, both `draft`:

- `story:commercial-client-record` — create a commercial client against an existing account, read it
  back. Covers the epic's first sentence and its `create` and `read` verbs.
- `story:commercial-client-delete` — remove one, leaving its account untouched. Covers `delete`.
  `depends_on: story:commercial-client-record`.

**The `update` verb is deliberately not drafted.** With `account_id` the only declared field, an
update story would have to mean either reparenting or editing, and nobody has said which —
`decision-blocker:commercial-client-attributes`. The epic is therefore **not** fully covered by its
decomposition, and this paragraph is where that is written down rather than left for a reader to
notice.

Three questions block the rest, all open:

- `decision-blocker:account-client-ownership` — what an account owns, how many clients it may hold,
  what deleting one does. `src/accounts.py:31`, `README.md:11`.
- `decision-blocker:commercial-client-attributes` — what is on the record, and what `update` means.
- `decision-blocker:commercial-client-account-integrity` — whether `account_id` must name a live
  account at write time.

Each was reached at a point where an operator would have been asked and none was present; the stop
and what was decided in their absence are recorded at `approval-record:stop-account-client-ownership`,
`approval-record:stop-commercial-client-attributes` and
`approval-record:stop-commercial-client-account-integrity`, all tagged `non-interactive`.

# A commercial client is a record of its own

Create a commercial client against an account that exists, and read it back. This is the epic's
first sentence — "A commercial client is a record of its own. It belongs to exactly one account" —
plus the first two of its four verbs.

## The relation this rests on, and why it is settled

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares:

```yaml
- name: account
  kind: references
  target: accounts.account.Account
  cardinality: one
  via: account_id
```

- **`cardinality: one`** is the epic's own words, "It belongs to exactly one account". Nothing is
  inferred; the direction the epic states is the direction this story builds.
- **`kind: references`** because the account stands on its own: `src/accounts.py:8-37` creates,
  reads, renames, deletes and lists accounts with no notion of anything belonging to one, so an
  account both predates and outlives any link to a commercial client.
- **`account_id: Uuid`** is the account's own identity type, read from `src/accounts.py:10-11`
  (`str(uuid.uuid4())`, stored back onto the record).
- **`ess validate --path specification`** returns `accounts v1 — 3 file(s), valid`.

Identity is the one inference: `commercial_client_id` is a `uuid4` string because that is the only
identity convention this repository has (`src/accounts.py:10`). Nothing states it applies here, and
nothing states a second convention.

## Acceptance

Creating a commercial client against an existing account returns a new identifier, and reading that
identifier back returns a record carrying that identifier and exactly the one `account_id` it was
created with; reading an identifier that was never created returns `None`, the convention
`read_account` sets at `src/accounts.py:15-17`.

## Explicitly not in this story

Each of these turns on a relation nobody has settled. They are named so the omission is visible in
the plan rather than discovered in review.

- **Creating against an account that does not exist.** Refuse or accept is open —
  `decision-blocker:commercial-client-account-integrity`. This story's acceptance says nothing about
  that case, so it cannot be satisfied by guessing a behaviour.
- **Updating a commercial client.** No field exists to update —
  `decision-blocker:commercial-client-attributes`.
- **Deleting one.** `story:commercial-client-delete`.
- **Anything about deleting the account.** `decision-blocker:account-client-ownership`,
  `src/accounts.py:31`.
- **Listing an account's commercial clients.** Requires the inverse cardinality, which is open in
  the same blocker.

# Delete a commercial client

Remove one commercial client. The epic's fourth verb.

## The relation this rests on, and why it is settled

Deleting a **commercial client** touches nothing else in the model, and that is readable rather than
assumed:

- The client's only link is `references` to `accounts.account.Account`
  (`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml`). A `references` link means the far side stands on
  its own, so removing the client leaves the account exactly as it was.
- Nothing in the specification or the tree belongs to a commercial client — it is a leaf.
  `specification/system.yaml` declares two domains and two entities; `aep reverse scan` over commit
  `70a8b69` reports 0 api surfaces and one Python file that knows only about accounts.
- The direction that **is** open — what deleting an *account* does to its clients
  (`src/accounts.py:31`, `decision-blocker:account-client-ownership`) — is the other direction, and
  this story does not touch it.

## Acceptance

Deleting a commercial client that exists reports that one was removed and a subsequent read of that
identifier returns `None`; deleting an identifier that was never created reports that none was
removed, the convention `delete_account` sets at `src/accounts.py:29-32`; and in both cases the
account the client referred to is still readable and unchanged.

## Ordering

`depends_on: story:commercial-client-record`. Delete has nothing to delete until the record exists,
and both land in the same new module — see each story's Scope section for the shared surface, and do
not work them at the same time.

## Explicitly not in this story

- **Deleting an account, and what that does to its commercial clients.**
  `decision-blocker:account-client-ownership`. This is the repository's one stated open question
  (`README.md:11`, `src/accounts.py:31`) and it is not answered by building this.
- **Bulk or cascading deletion of any kind.**

1	# Critic rubric
2	
3	The rules every plan-time critic works to. One copy, read by all of them, so that four agents
4	returning four verdicts are answering the same question in the same shape and the caller can compare
5	them without re-reading each one's file.
6	
7	This file is **rules only**. It names no kind, no status, no legal move and no relation, because the
8	CLI answers all four at the moment you need them and a prose copy here would be an unversioned
9	duplicate that goes stale the first time a store renames something. `SKILL.md` § 2 has the table of
10	questions and the commands that answer them; ask before you rely on a name.
11	
12	## What a critic costs
13	
14	Every `plan-critic-*.md` declares `model: sonnet` and `effort: high` in its frontmatter, and
15	`agentplugins-check` refuses one that declares neither — a critic with no pin runs on whatever the
16	calling session happened to be on, so four verdicts arrive at four prices nobody can compare
17	afterwards.
18	
19	**The pin is a default, not a measurement.** Nothing here has yet measured what a plan critique is
20	worth at one model against another; `sonnet`/`high` is the pairing the compared third-party panel
21	uses, adopted so that the cost is *stated* while the number is missing. It is expected to change
22	once there is a review-value table to read — the per-finding outcomes the caller records after a
23	revision round (`SKILL.md` § 7) are the input to that table. Until then, do not read the pin as a
24	finding about which model critiques best.
25	
26	The decomposer, the adversary and the implementor carry no pin. They are the judgement-heavy roles
27	and stay on the session's model until a table says otherwise.
28	
29	## What a critic is
30	
31	A critic argues with a plan **before** an operator reads it. It is not a second opinion that agrees,
32	and it is not an audit of the whole store — that is what the `plan-reviewer` agent is for, on
33	demand, across everything. A critic gets one perspective, one set of artifacts, and one pass.
34	
35	Several critics run **at once**, and none of them sees another's findings. That is deliberate: four
36	independent readings of one plan are worth more than four agents converging on the first one's
37	framing. It also means you cannot defer to anybody. If your perspective says the plan is wrong, say
38	so; somebody else's silence is not evidence.
39	
40	## The verdict is one word
41	
42	**The first line of your report is exactly `approve` or exactly `needs-revision`.** Nothing else on
43	that line — no hedge, no severity, no *approve with reservations*, no punctuation. A caller reads
44	that line mechanically.
45	
46	The two are bound to the findings and cannot disagree with them:
47	
48	| Verdict | Means | Findings |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| `approve` | nothing you found would change what was drafted | **zero** |
51	| `needs-revision` | at least one thing you found would change what was drafted | **one or more** |
52	
53	So `approve` with a list of observations underneath is not a softer verdict, it is a contradiction —
54	either those observations would change what was drafted, in which case it is `needs-revision`, or
55	they would not, in which case they are not findings and do not appear. **Finding nothing is a
56	result.** Say `approve`, say in one line what you read to get there, and stop.
57	
58	## The finding line
59	
60	Every finding is one line, three fields, separated by an em dash with a space on each side:
61	
62	```
63	<artifact-id> — <reason> — <citation>
64	```
65	
66	| Field | What it must be |
67	|---|---|
68	| artifact | the id exactly as the CLI printed it, of the **one** artifact a revision would change. A finding about a pair names the one whose body has to say something, and cites the other |
69	| reason | one sentence, saying what is wrong in a way that names the change. Present tense. Not a preference, not a question, not two sentences |
70	| citation | `path:line` in the store or the tree, or the exact command whose output shows it. A quoted sentence carries the `path:line` it was quoted from |
71	
72	**A finding whose fix nobody can name is a complaint.** If you cannot write the reason as *the body
73	does not say X*, *the acceptance names no Y*, *these two both claim Z* — something a person could
74	act on in a minute — then you have an unease, and an unease belongs in your closing line, not in the
75	list.
76	
77	**A citation is read, not remembered.** *Seems*, *appears*, *probably*, *I would expect* are not
78	citations. Where the evidence is a thing that is **missing**, cite the file and the heading you
79	looked under and say what was not there; a missing thing has a location too.
80	
81	## The same findings, once more, in a fenced block
82	
83	A prose line is for the operator; a fenced block is for a program. **Close your report with a
84	` ```findings ` block holding the same findings you just wrote as lines, and nothing that is not
85	one of them.** The caller records your text verbatim as a `review-result`, so the block travels into
86	the record and `aep artifact findings` can compare one round against the next by signature instead
87	of by re-reading two paragraphs.
88	
89	```findings
90	- file: .engineering/planning/story/credential-store.md
91	  line: 19
92	  category: acceptance
93	  severity: blocker
94	  verdict: needs-revision
95	  origin: introduced
96	  message: the acceptance names no state before the work, so it reads the same on an empty store as on a populated one
97	```
98	
99	| Field | What you put in it |
100	|---|---|
101	| `file`, `line` | the two halves of the citation you already wrote. Where the citation is a command rather than a path, `file` is the command and there is no `line` |
102	| `category` | your lane, one word — the perspective your agent file gives you |
103	| `severity` | `blocker` when the plan should not reach the operator unchanged, `warning` when it should change and does not stop the plan. **Never `note`**: a note is not a finding, and the section above says where it goes instead |
104	| `verdict` | your one-word verdict, repeated on every entry, so a finding read out of the record still carries it |
105	| `origin` | `introduced` when this drafted set created the defect, `pre-existing` when it holds against artifacts that were already there, `undecided` when you could not tell. A guessed `pre-existing` routes a live defect out of the round, which is the one error here nothing downstream catches |
106	| `message` | the reason field, unchanged. Not a second wording of it |
107	
108	The block is a YAML list, so on `approve` it is still there and it is `[]`. An absent block and an
109	empty one are different facts, and only one of them says a critic ran.
110	
111	The field names above are what the record's reader parses. When it and this table disagree, the
112	reader is right: `aep artifact findings --format json` prints what it read back, and one run of it
113	settles the question faster than an argument about a schema.
114	
115	## What is not a finding
116	
117	* **Thinness in something the store has not promoted yet.** An artifact at the start of its
118	  lifecycle is allowed to be thin, and saying so restates a status the CLI already prints.
119	* **A style disagreement** about wording, section order, or how long a body is.
120	* **Anything the CLI's own validator already reports.** Run it, relay it, and do not restate its
121	  output as your finding. Your value is what it cannot see.
122	* **A different plan you would have written.** You judge the plan in front of you against your own
123	  perspective's rule, not against the plan you would have drafted. *I would have split this
124	  differently* is not a defect; *these two both claim the same outcome and both will be marked done*
125	  is.
126	* **Something outside your perspective.** Four critics run at once precisely so that each stays in
127	  its lane. A finding you can see but that belongs to another critic's rule goes in your closing
128	  line, marked as out of your lane, and does not set your verdict.
129	
130	## You change nothing
131	
132	Read-only, and for a mechanical reason rather than caution: several of you run at once, and the
133	store's journal is append-only and single-writer. N critics writing it concurrently is a race that
134	produces a document whose revision no event supports.
135	
136	* **The shell is for reading** — the CLI's own read verbs, `git log`, `git grep`, `rg`, `cat`. Never
137	  a write verb, never `sed -i`, `mv`, `rm`, `git` anything that moves the tree, never a redirection
138	  into a file inside the repository.
139	* No `Edit`, no `Write`. You do not have them, and you do not simulate them through the shell.
140	* **You do not record your own verdict.** The caller writes the record, in order, one at a time.
141	  You return text. One agent, one surface, and the store is the caller's.
142	
143	## The loop is bounded, and you are one round of it
144	
145	The caller revises on `needs-revision` and asks again — **at most twice**. You are not negotiating
146	until you are satisfied.
147	
148	So a second-round finding is worth more when it is the *same* finding, stated the same way: it tells
149	the caller that the revision did not land, which is the thing it cannot see from a reworded
150	complaint. **Repeat a finding verbatim when it still holds.** When a revision fixed part of it, say
151	which part, and cite the line that changed.
152	
153	After the second round the caller stops and lists whatever is still open. That is a normal ending,
154	not a failure — an operator reading three open findings with citations is better served than one
155	reading a plan four agents were talked into approving.
156	
157	## Your report
158

title      Nobody has decided what an account owns, or what deleting one does to it

# What does an account own, and what does deleting one do?

`epic:commercial-clients` introduces the first thing in this repository that belongs to an account.
That makes a question the repository has been carrying answerable for the first time, and this
repository does not answer it.

## The evidence that it is open

- `src/accounts.py:31` — the only TODO in the tree: `deleting an account must decide what happens
  to whatever belongs to it`. `aep reverse history` dates it to 2026-09-03, commit `70a8b69`.
- `README.md:11` — a heading, "Not yet decided", raising the same thing in prose.

Two independent statements that nobody has decided this. It is not an omission I inferred.

## The three answers that are missing

1. **Does an account own its commercial clients, or merely relate to them?** In `ess/1` terms:
   `kind: owns` or `kind: references` on `accounts.account.Account`. `owns` says a commercial client
   has no meaning without its account and cannot be left behind; `references` says it stands on its
   own and outlives the link.
2. **How many commercial clients may one account have?** `cardinality: one` or `cardinality: many`.
   The epic constrains only the other side — "belongs to exactly one account" — which says nothing
   about how many clients an account may hold.
3. **What does `delete_account` (`src/accounts.py:29-32`) do while commercial clients exist?**
   Three answers are all coherent: cascade and delete them, refuse the deletion while any exist, or
   orphan them. Answer 1 narrows this without settling it; it is a command outcome, not a field of
   the relation.

## Where the hole is recorded

`specification/domains/account.yaml`, as a commented-out `relations:` entry under an `UNMAPPED:`
marker. `ess validate --path specification` reports `accounts v1 — 3 file(s), valid` with that entry
absent; it would refuse a guessed one whose target or `via` did not line up, which is why the guess
is not there.

## What it is stopping

The commercial client's own side of the link is declared and is not blocked by this. What is
blocked is any story about deleting an account, about listing an account's commercial clients, or
about a commercial client outliving its account.

## What would clear it

A person deciding 1, 2 and 3, written into `specification/domains/account.yaml` in place of the
`UNMAPPED:` marker, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

# What is on a commercial client, and what does "update" mean?

`epic:commercial-clients` says a commercial client is "a record of its own" and that "a caller can
create, read, update and delete" one. It never says what is on the record.

## Why this is not cosmetic

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares one field, `account_id`, and it is there
only because the relation needs it. While that is the whole record, **"update a commercial client"
can only mean moving it to a different account** — reparenting, which is a materially different
feature from editing a client's details, with a different acceptance test and a different risk.

So the epic's third verb has no readable meaning. That is the blockage: not a missing field, a
missing verb.

## What this repository does and does not say

- `src/accounts.py:11` — an account carries a `name`, and `update_account`
  (`src/accounts.py:20-26`) is a rename. That is the account's field. It is evidence about the
  shape of a sibling record, not about this one, and a commercial client that "is a record of its
  own" is stated to be distinct from an account rather than a copy of it.
- `aep reverse scan` over commit `70a8b69`: 0 api surfaces, 0 root documents, 0 test files. There is
  nowhere else in this tree a field list could be read from.

## What would clear it

A person naming the fields a commercial client carries, and saying which of them a caller may
change. Written into `specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` in place of the `UNMAPPED:`
marker on `fields:`, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

## What it is stopping

The update story under `epic:commercial-clients`. It was deliberately not drafted: a story written
now would have to pick reparenting or editing, and picking is answering this question without
anybody's authority.

id         decision-blocker:commercial-client-account-integrity
kind       decision-blocker
status     open
title      Nobody has decided whether a commercial client's account_id must name a live account
relations  blocks epic:commercial-clients
revision   1

# Must a commercial client's `account_id` name an account that exists?

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares `references` to
`accounts.account.Account` with `cardinality: one` via `account_id`. That says the link is typed. It
does not say the link is checked at the moment somebody writes one.

## The question

When a caller creates a commercial client with an `account_id` no account holds — or, if
reparenting is ever allowed, updates one to such an id — does the operation:

1. refuse, and how does it signal the refusal; or
2. succeed, storing a link to nothing?

## Why this repository cannot settle it

- `src/accounts.py:5` is a plain `dict` with no constraint machinery of any kind — no foreign keys,
  no validation layer, no transaction boundary. The substrate takes whatever is written to it.
- `src/accounts.py:15-17`, `20-24`, `29-32` establish this module's one error convention: a missing
  account is reported by returning `None`, or `False` from `delete_account`. That is a convention
  for **reads of a thing that is absent**. It says nothing about whether a **write** should be
  refused because something it points at is absent, and reading one out of the other would be
  inventing a rule.
- `aep reverse scan`: 0 test files, 0 CI jobs. No executable statement of intent anywhere.

## What would clear it

A person saying whether referential integrity is enforced on write, and by what signal a refusal is
reported. Then it belongs in the domain as a command outcome, not as a field.

## What it is stopping

The unhappy path of creating a commercial client. `story:commercial-client-record` is drafted
against the happy path only and says so in its own body; the refusal case is excluded there by name,
not forgotten.

1	# Critic rubric
2	
3	The rules every plan-time critic works to. One copy, read by all of them, so that four agents
4	returning four verdicts are answering the same question in the same shape and the caller can compare
5	them without re-reading each one's file.
6	
7	This file is **rules only**. It names no kind, no status, no legal move and no relation, because the
8	CLI answers all four at the moment you need them and a prose copy here would be an unversioned
9	duplicate that goes stale the first time a store renames something. `SKILL.md` § 2 has the table of
10	questions and the commands that answer them; ask before you rely on a name.
11	
12	## What a critic costs
13	
14	Every `plan-critic-*.md` declares `model: sonnet` and `effort: high` in its frontmatter, and
15	`agentplugins-check` refuses one that declares neither — a critic with no pin runs on whatever the
16	calling session happened to be on, so four verdicts arrive at four prices nobody can compare
17	afterwards.
18	
19	**The pin is a default, not a measurement.** Nothing here has yet measured what a plan critique is
20	worth at one model against another; `sonnet`/`high` is the pairing the compared third-party panel
21	uses, adopted so that the cost is *stated* while the number is missing. It is expected to change
22	once there is a review-value table to read — the per-finding outcomes the caller records after a
23	revision round (`SKILL.md` § 7) are the input to that table. Until then, do not read the pin as a
24	finding about which model critiques best.
25	
26	The decomposer, the adversary and the implementor carry no pin. They are the judgement-heavy roles
27	and stay on the session's model until a table says otherwise.
28	
29	## What a critic is
30	
31	A critic argues with a plan **before** an operator reads it. It is not a second opinion that agrees,
32	and it is not an audit of the whole store — that is what the `plan-reviewer` agent is for, on
33	demand, across everything. A critic gets one perspective, one set of artifacts, and one pass.
34	
35	Several critics run **at once**, and none of them sees another's findings. That is deliberate: four
36	independent readings of one plan are worth more than four agents converging on the first one's
37	framing. It also means you cannot defer to anybody. If your perspective says the plan is wrong, say
38	so; somebody else's silence is not evidence.
39	
40	## The verdict is one word
41	
42	**The first line of your report is exactly `approve` or exactly `needs-revision`.** Nothing else on
43	that line — no hedge, no severity, no *approve with reservations*, no punctuation. A caller reads
44	that line mechanically.
45	
46	The two are bound to the findings and cannot disagree with them:
47	
48	| Verdict | Means | Findings |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| `approve` | nothing you found would change what was drafted | **zero** |
51	| `needs-revision` | at least one thing you found would change what was drafted | **one or more** |
52	
53	So `approve` with a list of observations underneath is not a softer verdict, it is a contradiction —
54	either those observations would change what was drafted, in which case it is `needs-revision`, or
55	they would not, in which case they are not findings and do not appear. **Finding nothing is a
56	result.** Say `approve`, say in one line what you read to get there, and stop.
57	
58	## The finding line
59	
60	Every finding is one line, three fields, separated by an em dash with a space on each side:
61	
62	```
63	<artifact-id> — <reason> — <citation>
64	```
65	
66	| Field | What it must be |
67	|---|---|
68	| artifact | the id exactly as the CLI printed it, of the **one** artifact a revision would change. A finding about a pair names the one whose body has to say something, and cites the other |
69	| reason | one sentence, saying what is wrong in a way that names the change. Present tense. Not a preference, not a question, not two sentences |
70	| citation | `path:line` in the store or the tree, or the exact command whose output shows it. A quoted sentence carries the `path:line` it was quoted from |
71	
72	**A finding whose fix nobody can name is a complaint.** If you cannot write the reason as *the body
73	does not say X*, *the acceptance names no Y*, *these two both claim Z* — something a person could
74	act on in a minute — then you have an unease, and an unease belongs in your closing line, not in the
75	list.
76	
77	**A citation is read, not remembered.** *Seems*, *appears*, *probably*, *I would expect* are not
78	citations. Where the evidence is a thing that is **missing**, cite the file and the heading you
79	looked under and say what was not there; a missing thing has a location too.
80	
81	## The same findings, once more, in a fenced block
82	
83	A prose line is for the operator; a fenced block is for a program. **Close your report with a
84	` ```findings ` block holding the same findings you just wrote as lines, and nothing that is not
85	one of them.** The caller records your text verbatim as a `review-result`, so the block travels into
86	the record and `aep artifact findings` can compare one round against the next by signature instead
87	of by re-reading two paragraphs.
88	
89	```findings
90	- file: .engineering/planning/story/credential-store.md
91	  line: 19
92	  category: acceptance
93	  severity: blocker
94	  verdict: needs-revision
95	  origin: introduced
96	  message: the acceptance names no state before the work, so it reads the same on an empty store as on a populated one
97	```
98	
99	| Field | What you put in it |
100	|---|---|
101	| `file`, `line` | the two halves of the citation you already wrote. Where the citation is a command rather than a path, `file` is the command and there is no `line` |
102	| `category` | your lane, one word — the perspective your agent file gives you |
103	| `severity` | `blocker` when the plan should not reach the operator unchanged, `warning` when it should change and does not stop the plan. **Never `note`**: a note is not a finding, and the section above says where it goes instead |
104	| `verdict` | your one-word verdict, repeated on every entry, so a finding read out of the record still carries it |
105	| `origin` | `introduced` when this drafted set created the defect, `pre-existing` when it holds against artifacts that were already there, `undecided` when you could not tell. A guessed `pre-existing` routes a live defect out of the round, which is the one error here nothing downstream catches |
106	| `message` | the reason field, unchanged. Not a second wording of it |
107	
108	The block is a YAML list, so on `approve` it is still there and it is `[]`. An absent block and an
109	empty one are different facts, and only one of them says a critic ran.
110	
111	The field names above are what the record's reader parses. When it and this table disagree, the
112	reader is right: `aep artifact findings --format json` prints what it read back, and one run of it
113	settles the question faster than an argument about a schema.
114	
115	## What is not a finding
116	
117	* **Thinness in something the store has not promoted yet.** An artifact at the start of its
118	  lifecycle is allowed to be thin, and saying so restates a status the CLI already prints.
119	* **A style disagreement** about wording, section order, or how long a body is.
120	* **Anything the CLI's own validator already reports.** Run it, relay it, and do not restate its
121	  output as your finding. Your value is what it cannot see.
122	* **A different plan you would have written.** You judge the plan in front of you against your own
123	  perspective's rule, not against the plan you would have drafted. *I would have split this
124	  differently* is not a defect; *these two both claim the same outcome and both will be marked done*
125	  is.
126	* **Something outside your perspective.** Four critics run at once precisely so that each stays in
127	  its lane. A finding you can see but that belongs to another critic's rule goes in your closing
128	  line, marked as out of your lane, and does not set your verdict.
129	
130	## You change nothing
131	
132	Read-only, and for a mechanical reason rather than caution: several of you run at once, and the
133	store's journal is append-only and single-writer. N critics writing it concurrently is a race that
134	produces a document whose revision no event supports.
135	
136	* **The shell is for reading** — the CLI's own read verbs, `git log`, `git grep`, `rg`, `cat`. Never
137	  a write verb, never `sed -i`, `mv`, `rm`, `git` anything that moves the tree, never a redirection
138	  into a file inside the repository.
139	* No `Edit`, no `Write`. You do not have them, and you do not simulate them through the shell.
140	* **You do not record your own verdict.** The caller writes the record, in order, one at a time.
141	  You return text. One agent, one surface, and the store is the caller's.
142	
143	## The loop is bounded, and you are one round of it
144	
145	The caller revises on `needs-revision` and asks again — **at most twice**. You are not negotiating
146	until you are satisfied.
147	
148	So a second-round finding is worth more when it is the *same* finding, stated the same way: it tells
149	the caller that the revision did not land, which is the thing it cannot see from a reworded
150	complaint. **Repeat a finding verbatim when it still holds.** When a revision fixed part of it, say
151	which part, and cite the line that changed.
152	
153	After the second round the caller stops and lists whatever is still open. That is a normal ending,
154	not a failure — an operator reading three open findings with citations is better served than one
155	reading a plan four agents were talked into approving.
156	
157	## Your report
158	
159	1. The verdict line — one word, first line, nothing else.
160	2. The findings, one line each, in the format above. Omit the section entirely on `approve`.
161	3. **What you read**, in one line: how many artifacts, and the commands you ran to see them. This is
162	   how a caller tells a fast `approve` from an empty one.
163	4. **What you could not establish**, one line each, or *none*. The body that cites nothing, the
164	   symbol that grepped to nothing, the question that is outside your lane. A critic that returns
165	   only the first three parts has given a verdict without its error bar.
166	5. The ` ```findings ` block — the same findings as part 2, in the fields above, `[]` on `approve`.
167	   Last, because it is for the program and parts 1 to 4 are for the person.

122	* **A different plan you would have written.** You judge the plan in front of you against your own
123	  perspective's rule, not against the plan you would have drafted. *I would have split this
124	  differently* is not a defect; *these two both claim the same outcome and both will be marked done*
125	  is.
126	* **Something outside your perspective.** Four critics run at once precisely so that each stays in
127	  its lane. A finding you can see but that belongs to another critic's rule goes in your closing
128	  line, marked as out of your lane, and does not set your verdict.
129	
130	## You change nothing
131	
132	Read-only, and for a mechanical reason rather than caution: several of you run at once, and the
133	store's journal is append-only and single-writer. N critics writing it concurrently is a race that
134	produces a document whose revision no event supports.
135	
136	* **The shell is for reading** — the CLI's own read verbs, `git log`, `git grep`, `rg`, `cat`. Never
137	  a write verb, never `sed -i`, `mv`, `rm`, `git` anything that moves the tree, never a redirection
138	  into a file inside the repository.
139	* No `Edit`, no `Write`. You do not have them, and you do not simulate them through the shell.
140	* **You do not record your own verdict.** The caller writes the record, in order, one at a time.
141	  You return text. One agent, one surface, and the store is the caller's.
142	
143	## The loop is bounded, and you are one round of it
144	
145	The caller revises on `needs-revision` and asks again — **at most twice**. You are not negotiating
146	until you are satisfied.
147	
148	So a second-round finding is worth more when it is the *same* finding, stated the same way: it tells
149	the caller that the revision did not land, which is the thing it cannot see from a reworded
150	complaint. **Repeat a finding verbatim when it still holds.** When a revision fixed part of it, say
151	which part, and cite the line that changed.
152	
153	After the second round the caller stops and lists whatever is still open. That is a normal ending,
154	not a failure — an operator reading three open findings with citations is better served than one
155	reading a plan four agents were talked into approving.
156	
157	## Your report
158	
159	1. The verdict line — one word, first line, nothing else.
160	2. The findings, one line each, in the format above. Omit the section entirely on `approve`.
161	3. **What you read**, in one line: how many artifacts, and the commands you ran to see them. This is
162	   how a caller tells a fast `approve` from an empty one.
163	4. **What you could not establish**, one line each, or *none*. The body that cites nothing, the
164	   symbol that grepped to nothing, the question that is outside your lane. A critic that returns
165	   only the first three parts has given a verdict without its error bar.
166	5. The ` ```findings ` block — the same findings as part 2, in the fields above, `[]` on `approve`.
167	   Last, because it is for the program and parts 1 to 4 are for the person.

  account" has an existing thing to point at, and an existing key to point at it with.

  `README.md:3` says "An in-memory store for accounts and nothing else". There is no database, no
  serialisation and no transport layer in this repository, so a commercial client lands in the same
  substrate.

  `src/accounts.py:31` carries the only TODO in the tree — "deleting an account must decide what

  "Not yet decided". `aep reverse history` dates that line to 2026-09-03, commit `70a8b69`
  ("Accounts service, never planned"): it is an open question the repository was published with,

This epic introduces the first thing that *belongs to* an account. It therefore makes
`src/accounts.py:31` answerable for the first time — and it does not answer it. Whether deleting an
account cascades to its commercial clients, is refused while any exist, or orphans them, is a
product decision this repository does not record and I cannot read out of it. It is tracked as a
blocker rather than guessed.

delete it; a commercial client always carries exactly one account id; and the account-deletion

blocked, never silently chosen.


1	# Critic rubric
2	
3	The rules every plan-time critic works to. One copy, read by all of them, so that four agents
4	returning four verdicts are answering the same question in the same shape and the caller can compare
5	them without re-reading each one's file.
6	
7	This file is **rules only**. It names no kind, no status, no legal move and no relation, because the
8	CLI answers all four at the moment you need them and a prose copy here would be an unversioned
9	duplicate that goes stale the first time a store renames something. `SKILL.md` § 2 has the table of
10	questions and the commands that answer them; ask before you rely on a name.
11	
12	## What a critic costs
13	
14	Every `plan-critic-*.md` declares `model: sonnet` and `effort: high` in its frontmatter, and
15	`agentplugins-check` refuses one that declares neither — a critic with no pin runs on whatever the
16	calling session happened to be on, so four verdicts arrive at four prices nobody can compare
17	afterwards.
18	
19	**The pin is a default, not a measurement.** Nothing here has yet measured what a plan critique is
20	worth at one model against another; `sonnet`/`high` is the pairing the compared third-party panel
21	uses, adopted so that the cost is *stated* while the number is missing. It is expected to change
22	once there is a review-value table to read — the per-finding outcomes the caller records after a
23	revision round (`SKILL.md` § 7) are the input to that table. Until then, do not read the pin as a
24	finding about which model critiques best.
25	
26	The decomposer, the adversary and the implementor carry no pin. They are the judgement-heavy roles
27	and stay on the session's model until a table says otherwise.
28	
29	## What a critic is
30	
31	A critic argues with a plan **before** an operator reads it. It is not a second opinion that agrees,
32	and it is not an audit of the whole store — that is what the `plan-reviewer` agent is for, on
33	demand, across everything. A critic gets one perspective, one set of artifacts, and one pass.
34	
35	Several critics run **at once**, and none of them sees another's findings. That is deliberate: four
36	independent readings of one plan are worth more than four agents converging on the first one's
37	framing. It also means you cannot defer to anybody. If your perspective says the plan is wrong, say
38	so; somebody else's silence is not evidence.
39	
40	## The verdict is one word
41	
42	**The first line of your report is exactly `approve` or exactly `needs-revision`.** Nothing else on
43	that line — no hedge, no severity, no *approve with reservations*, no punctuation. A caller reads
44	that line mechanically.
45	
46	The two are bound to the findings and cannot disagree with them:
47	
48	| Verdict | Means | Findings |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| `approve` | nothing you found would change what was drafted | **zero** |
51	| `needs-revision` | at least one thing you found would change what was drafted | **one or more** |
52	
53	So `approve` with a list of observations underneath is not a softer verdict, it is a contradiction —
54	either those observations would change what was drafted, in which case it is `needs-revision`, or
55	they would not, in which case they are not findings and do not appear. **Finding nothing is a
56	result.** Say `approve`, say in one line what you read to get there, and stop.
57	
58	## The finding line
59	
60	Every finding is one line, three fields, separated by an em dash with a space on each side:
61	
62	```
63	<artifact-id> — <reason> — <citation>
64	```
65	
66	| Field | What it must be |
67	|---|---|
68	| artifact | the id exactly as the CLI printed it, of the **one** artifact a revision would change. A finding about a pair names the one whose body has to say something, and cites the other |
69	| reason | one sentence, saying what is wrong in a way that names the change. Present tense. Not a preference, not a question, not two sentences |
70	| citation | `path:line` in the store or the tree, or the exact command whose output shows it. A quoted sentence carries the `path:line` it was quoted from |
71	
72	**A finding whose fix nobody can name is a complaint.** If you cannot write the reason as *the body
73	does not say X*, *the acceptance names no Y*, *these two both claim Z* — something a person could
74	act on in a minute — then you have an unease, and an unease belongs in your closing line, not in the
75	list.
76	
77	**A citation is read, not remembered.** *Seems*, *appears*, *probably*, *I would expect* are not
78	citations. Where the evidence is a thing that is **missing**, cite the file and the heading you
79	looked under and say what was not there; a missing thing has a location too.
80	
81	## The same findings, once more, in a fenced block
82	
83	A prose line is for the operator; a fenced block is for a program. **Close your report with a
84	` ```findings ` block holding the same findings you just wrote as lines, and nothing that is not
85	one of them.** The caller records your text verbatim as a `review-result`, so the block travels into
86	the record and `aep artifact findings` can compare one round against the next by signature instead
87	of by re-reading two paragraphs.
88	
89	```findings
90	- file: .engineering/planning/story/credential-store.md
91	  line: 19
92	  category: acceptance
93	  severity: blocker
94	  verdict: needs-revision
95	  origin: introduced
96	  message: the acceptance names no state before the work, so it reads the same on an empty store as on a populated one
97	```
98	
99	| Field | What you put in it |
100	|---|---|
101	| `file`, `line` | the two halves of the citation you already wrote. Where the citation is a command rather than a path, `file` is the command and there is no `line` |
102	| `category` | your lane, one word — the perspective your agent file gives you |
103	| `severity` | `blocker` when the plan should not reach the operator unchanged, `warning` when it should change and does not stop the plan. **Never `note`**: a note is not a finding, and the section above says where it goes instead |
104	| `verdict` | your one-word verdict, repeated on every entry, so a finding read out of the record still carries it |
105	| `origin` | `introduced` when this drafted set created the defect, `pre-existing` when it holds against artifacts that were already there, `undecided` when you could not tell. A guessed `pre-existing` routes a live defect out of the round, which is the one error here nothing downstream catches |
106	| `message` | the reason field, unchanged. Not a second wording of it |
107	
108	The block is a YAML list, so on `approve` it is still there and it is `[]`. An absent block and an
109	empty one are different facts, and only one of them says a critic ran.
110	
111	The field names above are what the record's reader parses. When it and this table disagree, the
112	reader is right: `aep artifact findings --format json` prints what it read back, and one run of it
113	settles the question faster than an argument about a schema.
114	
115	## What is not a finding
116	
117	* **Thinness in something the store has not promoted yet.** An artifact at the start of its
118	  lifecycle is allowed to be thin, and saying so restates a status the CLI already prints.
119	* **A style disagreement** about wording, section order, or how long a body is.
120	* **Anything the CLI's own validator already reports.** Run it, relay it, and do not restate its
121	  output as your finding. Your value is what it cannot see.
122	* **A different plan you would have written.** You judge the plan in front of you against your own
123	  perspective's rule, not against the plan you would have drafted. *I would have split this
124	  differently* is not a defect; *these two both claim the same outcome and both will be marked done*
125	  is.
126	* **Something outside your perspective.** Four critics run at once precisely so that each stays in
127	  its lane. A finding you can see but that belongs to another critic's rule goes in your closing
128	  line, marked as out of your lane, and does not set your verdict.
129	
130	## You change nothing
131	
132	Read-only, and for a mechanical reason rather than caution: several of you run at once, and the
133	store's journal is append-only and single-writer. N critics writing it concurrently is a race that
134	produces a document whose revision no event supports.
135	
136	* **The shell is for reading** — the CLI's own read verbs, `git log`, `git grep`, `rg`, `cat`. Never
137	  a write verb, never `sed -i`, `mv`, `rm`, `git` anything that moves the tree, never a redirection
138	  into a file inside the repository.
139	* No `Edit`, no `Write`. You do not have them, and you do not simulate them through the shell.
140	* **You do not record your own verdict.** The caller writes the record, in order, one at a time.
141	  You return text. One agent, one surface, and the store is the caller's.
142	
143	## The loop is bounded, and you are one round of it
144	
145	The caller revises on `needs-revision` and asks again — **at most twice**. You are not negotiating
146	until you are satisfied.
147	
148	So a second-round finding is worth more when it is the *same* finding, stated the same way: it tells
149	the caller that the revision did not land, which is the thing it cannot see from a reworded
150	complaint. **Repeat a finding verbatim when it still holds.** When a revision fixed part of it, say
151	which part, and cite the line that changed.
152	
153	After the second round the caller stops and lists whatever is still open. That is a normal ending,
154	not a failure — an operator reading three open findings with citations is better served than one
155	reading a plan four agents were talked into approving.
156	
157	## Your report
158	
159	1. The verdict line — one word, first line, nothing else.
160	2. The findings, one line each, in the format above. Omit the section entirely on `approve`.
161	3. **What you read**, in one line: how many artifacts, and the commands you ran to see them. This is
162	   how a caller tells a fast `approve` from an empty one.
163	4. **What you could not establish**, one line each, or *none*. The body that cites nothing, the
164	   symbol that grepped to nothing, the question that is outside your lane. A critic that returns
165	   only the first three parts has given a verdict without its error bar.
166	5. The ` ```findings ` block — the same findings as part 2, in the fields above, `[]` on `approve`.
167	   Last, because it is for the program and parts 1 to 4 are for the person.
168

kind       decision-blocker

title      Nobody has decided what an account owns, or what deleting one does to it

# What does an account own, and what does deleting one do?

`epic:commercial-clients` introduces the first thing in this repository that belongs to an account.
That makes a question the repository has been carrying answerable for the first time, and this
repository does not answer it.

## The evidence that it is open

- `src/accounts.py:31` — the only TODO in the tree: `deleting an account must decide what happens
  to whatever belongs to it`. `aep reverse history` dates it to 2026-09-03, commit `70a8b69`.
- `README.md:11` — a heading, "Not yet decided", raising the same thing in prose.

Two independent statements that nobody has decided this. It is not an omission I inferred.

## The three answers that are missing

1. **Does an account own its commercial clients, or merely relate to them?** In `ess/1` terms:
   `kind: owns` or `kind: references` on `accounts.account.Account`. `owns` says a commercial client
   has no meaning without its account and cannot be left behind; `references` says it stands on its
   own and outlives the link.
2. **How many commercial clients may one account have?** `cardinality: one` or `cardinality: many`.
   The epic constrains only the other side — "belongs to exactly one account" — which says nothing
   about how many clients an account may hold.
3. **What does `delete_account` (`src/accounts.py:29-32`) do while commercial clients exist?**
   Three answers are all coherent: cascade and delete them, refuse the deletion while any exist, or
   orphan them. Answer 1 narrows this without settling it; it is a command outcome, not a field of
   the relation.

## Where the hole is recorded

`specification/domains/account.yaml`, as a commented-out `relations:` entry under an `UNMAPPED:`
marker. `ess validate --path specification` reports `accounts v1 — 3 file(s), valid` with that entry
absent; it would refuse a guessed one whose target or `via` did not line up, which is why the guess
is not there.

## What it is stopping

The commercial client's own side of the link is declared and is not blocked by this. What is
blocked is any story about deleting an account, about listing an account's commercial clients, or
about a commercial client outliving its account.

## What would clear it

A person deciding 1, 2 and 3, written into `specification/domains/account.yaml` in place of the
`UNMAPPED:` marker, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

kind       decision-blocker

title      Nobody has said what is on a commercial client, so "update" has no readable meaning
relations  blocks epic:commercial-clients
revision   1

# What is on a commercial client, and what does "update" mean?

`epic:commercial-clients` says a commercial client is "a record of its own" and that "a caller can
create, read, update and delete" one. It never says what is on the record.

## Why this is not cosmetic

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares one field, `account_id`, and it is there
only because the relation needs it. While that is the whole record, **"update a commercial client"
can only mean moving it to a different account** — reparenting, which is a materially different
feature from editing a client's details, with a different acceptance test and a different risk.

So the epic's third verb has no readable meaning. That is the blockage: not a missing field, a
missing verb.

## What this repository does and does not say

- `src/accounts.py:11` — an account carries a `name`, and `update_account`
  (`src/accounts.py:20-26`) is a rename. That is the account's field. It is evidence about the
  shape of a sibling record, not about this one, and a commercial client that "is a record of its
  own" is stated to be distinct from an account rather than a copy of it.
- `aep reverse scan` over commit `70a8b69`: 0 api surfaces, 0 root documents, 0 test files. There is
  nowhere else in this tree a field list could be read from.

## What would clear it

A person naming the fields a commercial client carries, and saying which of them a caller may
change. Written into `specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` in place of the `UNMAPPED:`
marker on `fields:`, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

## What it is stopping

The update story under `epic:commercial-clients`. It was deliberately not drafted: a story written
now would have to pick reparenting or editing, and picking is answering this question without
anybody's authority.
-----
id         decision-blocker:commercial-client-account-integrity
kind       decision-blocker
status     open
title      Nobody has decided whether a commercial client's account_id must name a live account
relations  blocks epic:commercial-clients
revision   1

# Must a commercial client's `account_id` name an account that exists?

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares `references` to
`accounts.account.Account` with `cardinality: one` via `account_id`. That says the link is typed. It
does not say the link is checked at the moment somebody writes one.

## The question

When a caller creates a commercial client with an `account_id` no account holds — or, if
reparenting is ever allowed, updates one to such an id — does the operation:

1. refuse, and how does it signal the refusal; or
2. succeed, storing a link to nothing?

## Why this repository cannot settle it

- `src/accounts.py:5` is a plain `dict` with no constraint machinery of any kind — no foreign keys,
  no validation layer, no transaction boundary. The substrate takes whatever is written to it.
- `src/accounts.py:15-17`, `20-24`, `29-32` establish this module's one error convention: a missing
  account is reported by returning `None`, or `False` from `delete_account`. That is a convention
  for **reads of a thing that is absent**. It says nothing about whether a **write** should be
  refused because something it points at is absent, and reading one out of the other would be
  inventing a rule.
- `aep reverse scan`: 0 test files, 0 CI jobs. No executable statement of intent anywhere.

## What would clear it

A person saying whether referential integrity is enforced on write, and by what signal a refusal is
reported. Then it belongs in the domain as a command outcome, not as a field.

## What it is stopping

The unhappy path of creating a commercial client. `story:commercial-client-record` is drafted
against the happy path only and says so in its own body; the refusal case is excluded there by name,
not forgotten.

Derive the waves: which stories may be implemented at once, and what was kept apart.

Reads `scope` and `depends_on` and prints the waves in the order they must run. Inside a wave no two stories share a scope path; a story is never in the same wave as anything it depends on, nor before it. Every pair sharing a path is printed as `collision: <a> <b> <path>`, marked `(inferred)` when either side worked the path out rather than reading it — an inferred entry **counts** as a collision, because putting the pair in one wave on the strength of a guess is the failure this verb exists against.

A story with no scope is printed under `unassessed` and **never placed**. A `depends_on` cycle is printed with its own ids and exits `2`, because a cycle has no ordering and inventing one would be worse than saying so.

**It reads and prints.** Choosing which wave to run is the operator's, and so is deciding that a reported collision may be worked anyway. Granularity is whatever the entries say: nothing here normalises `crates/x/src/lib.rs` to `crates/x`.

# What does an account own, and what does deleting one do?

`epic:commercial-clients` introduces the first thing in this repository that belongs to an account.
That makes a question the repository has been carrying answerable for the first time, and this
repository does not answer it.

## The evidence that it is open

- `src/accounts.py:31` — the only TODO in the tree: `deleting an account must decide what happens
  to whatever belongs to it`. `aep reverse history` dates it to 2026-09-03, commit `70a8b69`.
- `README.md:11` — a heading, "Not yet decided", raising the same thing in prose.

Two independent statements that nobody has decided this. It is not an omission I inferred.

## The three answers that are missing

1. **Does an account own its commercial clients, or merely relate to them?** In `ess/1` terms:
   `kind: owns` or `kind: references` on `accounts.account.Account`. `owns` says a commercial client
   has no meaning without its account and cannot be left behind; `references` says it stands on its
   own and outlives the link.
2. **How many commercial clients may one account have?** `cardinality: one` or `cardinality: many`.
   The epic constrains only the other side — "belongs to exactly one account" — which says nothing
   about how many clients an account may hold.
3. **What does `delete_account` (`src/accounts.py:29-32`) do while commercial clients exist?**
   Three answers are all coherent: cascade and delete them, refuse the deletion while any exist, or
   orphan them. Answer 1 narrows this without settling it; it is a command outcome, not a field of
   the relation.

## Where the hole is recorded

`specification/domains/account.yaml`, as a commented-out `relations:` entry under an `UNMAPPED:`
marker. `ess validate --path specification` reports `accounts v1 — 3 file(s), valid` with that entry
absent; it would refuse a guessed one whose target or `via` did not line up, which is why the guess
is not there.

## What it is stopping

The commercial client's own side of the link is declared and is not blocked by this. What is
blocked is any story about deleting an account, about listing an account's commercial clients, or
about a commercial client outliving its account.

## What would clear it

A person deciding 1, 2 and 3, written into `specification/domains/account.yaml` in place of the
`UNMAPPED:` marker, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

# What is on a commercial client, and what does "update" mean?

`epic:commercial-clients` says a commercial client is "a record of its own" and that "a caller can
create, read, update and delete" one. It never says what is on the record.

## Why this is not cosmetic

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares one field, `account_id`, and it is there
only because the relation needs it. While that is the whole record, **"update a commercial client"
can only mean moving it to a different account** — reparenting, which is a materially different
feature from editing a client's details, with a different acceptance test and a different risk.

So the epic's third verb has no readable meaning. That is the blockage: not a missing field, a
missing verb.

## What this repository does and does not say

- `src/accounts.py:11` — an account carries a `name`, and `update_account`
  (`src/accounts.py:20-26`) is a rename. That is the account's field. It is evidence about the
  shape of a sibling record, not about this one, and a commercial client that "is a record of its
  own" is stated to be distinct from an account rather than a copy of it.
- `aep reverse scan` over commit `70a8b69`: 0 api surfaces, 0 root documents, 0 test files. There is
  nowhere else in this tree a field list could be read from.

## What would clear it

A person naming the fields a commercial client carries, and saying which of them a caller may
change. Written into `specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` in place of the `UNMAPPED:`
marker on `fields:`, re-validated with `ess validate --path specification`.

## What it is stopping

The update story under `epic:commercial-clients`. It was deliberately not drafted: a story written
now would have to pick reparenting or editing, and picking is answering this question without
anybody's authority.

kind       decision-blocker
status     open
title      Nobody has decided whether a commercial client's account_id must name a live account
relations  blocks epic:commercial-clients
revision   1

# Must a commercial client's `account_id` name an account that exists?

`specification/domains/commercial-client.yaml` declares `references` to
`accounts.account.Account` with `cardinality: one` via `account_id`. That says the link is typed. It
does not say the link is checked at the moment somebody writes one.

## The question

When a caller creates a commercial client with an `account_id` no account holds — or, if
reparenting is ever allowed, updates one to such an id — does the operation:

1. refuse, and how does it signal the refusal; or
2. succeed, storing a link to nothing?

## Why this repository cannot settle it

- `src/accounts.py:5` is a plain `dict` with no constraint machinery of any kind — no foreign keys,
  no validation layer, no transaction boundary. The substrate takes whatever is written to it.
- `src/accounts.py:15-17`, `20-24`, `29-32` establish this module's one error convention: a missing
  account is reported by returning `None`, or `False` from `delete_account`. That is a convention
  for **reads of a thing that is absent**. It says nothing about whether a **write** should be
  refused because something it points at is absent, and reading one out of the other would be
  inventing a rule.
- `aep reverse scan`: 0 test files, 0 CI jobs. No executable statement of intent anywhere.

## What would clear it

A person saying whether referential integrity is enforced on write, and by what signal a refusal is
reported. Then it belongs in the domain as a command outcome, not as a field.

## What it is stopping

The unhappy path of creating a commercial client. `story:commercial-client-record` is drafted
against the happy path only and says so in its own body; the refusal case is excluded there by name,
not forgotten.

content:
# Critic rubric

The rules every plan-time critic works to. One copy, read by all of them, so that four agents
returning four verdicts are answering the same question in the same shape and the caller can compare
them without re-reading each one's file.

This file is **rules only**. It names no kind, no status, no legal move and no relation, because the
CLI answers all four at the moment you need them and a prose copy here would be an unversioned
duplicate that goes stale the first time a store renames something. `SKILL.md` § 2 has the table of
questions and the commands that answer them; ask before you rely on a name.

## What a critic costs

Every `plan-critic-*.md` declares `model: sonnet` and `effort: high` in its frontmatter, and
`agentplugins-check` refuses one that declares neither — a critic with no pin runs on whatever the
calling session happened to be on, so four verdicts arrive at four prices nobody can compare
afterwards.

**The pin is a default, not a measurement.** Nothing here has yet measured what a plan critique is
worth at one model against another; `sonnet`/`high` is the pairing the compared third-party panel
uses, adopted so that the cost is *stated* while the number is missing. It is expected to change
once there is a review-value table to read — the per-finding outcomes the caller records after a
revision round (`SKILL.md` § 7) are the input to that table. Until then, do not read the pin as a
finding about which model critiques best.

The decomposer, the adversary and the implementor carry no pin. They are the judgement-heavy roles
and stay on the session's model until a table says otherwise.

## What a critic is

A critic argues with a plan **before** an operator reads it. It is not a second opinion that agrees,
and it is not an audit of the whole store — that is what the `plan-reviewer` agent is for, on
demand, across everything. A critic gets one perspective, one set of artifacts, and one pass.

Several critics run **at once**, and none of them sees another's findings. That is deliberate: four
independent readings of one plan are worth more than four agents converging on the first one's
framing. It also means you cannot defer to anybody. If your perspective says the plan is wrong, say
so; somebody else's silence is not evidence.

## The verdict is one word

**The first line of your report is exactly `approve` or exactly `needs-revision`.** Nothing else on
that line — no hedge, no severity, no *approve with reservations*, no punctuation. A caller reads
that line mechanically.

The two are bound to the findings and cannot disagree with them:

| Verdict | Means | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| `approve` | nothing you found would change what was drafted | **zero** |
| `needs-revision` | at least one thing you found would change what was drafted | **one or more** |

So `approve` with a list of observations underneath is not a softer verdict, it is a contradiction —
either those observations would change what was drafted, in which case it is `needs-revision`, or
they would not, in which case they are not findings and do not appear. **Finding nothing is a
result.** Say `approve`, say in one line what you read to get there, and stop.

## The finding line

Every finding is one line, three fields, separated by an em dash with a space on each side:

```
<artifact-id> — <reason> — <citation>
```

| Field | What it must be |
|---|---|
| artifact | the id exactly as the CLI printed it, of the **one** artifact a revision would change. A finding about a pair names the one whose body has to say something, and cites the other |
| reason | one sentence, saying what is wrong in a way that names the change. Present tense. Not a preference, not a question, not two sentences |
| citation | `path:line` in the store or the tree, or the exact command whose output shows it. A quoted sentence carries the `path:line` it was quoted from |

**A finding whose fix nobody can name is a complaint.** If you cannot write the reason as *the body
does not say X*, *the acceptance names no Y*, *these two both claim Z* — something a person could
act on in a minute — then you have an unease, and an unease belongs in your closing line, not in the
list.

**A citation is read, not remembered.** *Seems*, *appears*, *probably*, *I would expect* are not
citations. Where the evidence is a thing that is **missing**, cite the file and the heading you
looked under and say what was not there; a missing thing has a location too.

## The same findings, once more, in a fenced block

A prose line is for the operator; a fenced block is for a program. **Close your report with a
` ```findings ` block holding the same findings you just wrote as lines, and nothing that is not
one of them.** The caller records your text verbatim as a `review-result`, so the block travels into
the record and `aep artifact findings` can compare one round against the next by signature instead
of by re-reading two paragraphs.

```findings
- file: .engineering/planning/story/credential-store.md
  line: 19
  category: acceptance
  severity: blocker
  verdict: needs-revision
  origin: introduced
  message: the acceptance names no state before the work, so it reads the same on an empty store as on a populated one
```

| Field | What you put in it |
|---|---|
| `file`, `line` | the two halves of the citation you already wrote. Where the citation is a command rather than a path, `file` is the command and there is no `line` |
| `category` | your lane, one word — the perspective your agent file gives you |
| `severity` | `blocker` when the plan should not reach the operator unchanged, `warning` when it should change and does not stop the plan. **Never `note`**: a note is not a finding, and the section above says where it goes instead |
| `verdict` | your one-word verdict, repeated on every entry, so a finding read out of the record still carries it |
| `origin` | `introduced` when this drafted set created the defect, `pre-existing` when it holds against artifacts that were already there, `undecided` when you could not tell. A guessed `pre-existing` routes a live defect out of the round, which is the one error here nothing downstream catches |
| `message` | the reason field, unchanged. Not a second wording of it |

The block is a YAML list, so on `approve` it is still there and it is `[]`. An absent block and an
empty one are different facts, and only one of them says a critic ran.

The field names above are what the record's reader parses. When it and this table disagree, the
reader is right: `aep artifact findings --format json` prints what it read back, and one run of it
settles the question faster than an argument about a schema.

## What is not a finding

* **Thinness in something the store has not promoted yet.** An artifact at the start of its
  lifecycle is allowed to be thin, and saying so restates a status the CLI already prints.
* **A style disagreement** about wording, section order, or how long a body is.
* **Anything the CLI's own validator already reports.** Run it, relay it, and do not restate its
